Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Gladstone) asked a question on October 22, as reported on page 1351 of Hansard, with regard to the use of firearms. I have received a report from the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police which will constitute an answer to the question.
Measures deemed to be appropriate have already been taken to control the entry of such souvenirs as revolvers, pistols, et cetera, into Canada by returning members of the Canadian armed forces.
The Department of National Defence (army, navy and air force) have all issued orders prohibiting the possession or retention of any weapons or ammunition taken from the enemy in the field during hostilities or after the cessation of hostilities. Any revolvers or auto-loading pistols which are brought back from overseas have to be registered in accordance with the provisions of the criminal code.
In addition, under the automatic firearms regulation, 1945, P.C. 4885, dated July 10, 1945, provision is made in this regulation banning the importation of automatic firearms. These automatic firearms are more commonly referred to as tommy guns. This regulation provides for the issuance of permits to allow persons to have such automatic firearms in their possession, but the commissioner has already issued orders to the effect that such permits are to be kept to an absolute minimum and issued only when the firearms in question have been rendered useless so that they cannot be used again for firing purposes.
Remarks were also made'in the house at the same time concerning defence of Canada regulation 37A. In this regard, while certain paragraphs of that regulation were revoked, thus removing from control of that regulation all firearms surrendered by aliens under war-time legislation, the control of such firearms comes under the criminal code, and it is encumbent upon such persons to obtain a permit in form 76B from the competent provincial authorities before they can legally regain possession [Mr. Mavbank.l

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Knight)

Labour Conditions
asked a question in regard to the transmission of parcels from Canada to Norway. I am glad to say that arrangements were completed a few days ago for the acceptance of such parcels, and instructions had already been issued in this connection when the hon. member addressed his question to the house yesterday.
This parcel post service has been placed in operation under the same conditions as at present applying to parcel post services from Canada to other countries on the continent to which such services have been resumed.
May I also make a statement, Mr. Speaker, on the removal of restrictions on the dispatch of newspapers and periodicals.
In August, 1942, in order to conserve shipping space, it was found necessary to prohibit the mailing of complete newspapers or periodicals to civilians and troops in the United Kingdom and other transatlantic destinations, as well as to destinations in Central and South America. Bermuda and the West Indies. Clippings of special interest were permitted. In January 1944, we were able to restore this service for mailings to Central America, South America, the Caribbean area and Bermuda, also to Africa via the United States, following the removal of the restrictions by the United States Post Office Department, through which service such mail was being forwarded.
Last May we were in a position to permit the mailing of newspapers, magazines and periodicals to members of the armed forces overseas, and now I am happy to say we are able to accept for onward transmission newspapers, magazines and periodicals to civilian addresses in the United Kingdom and other transatlantic destinations.
The effect of the foregoing, therefore, is the complete removal of the restrictions on the dispatch of newspapers and periodicals to overseas destinations.

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Perhaps I might reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Marshall) yesterday evening respecting the number of civil employees in the navy. He pointed out that in the auditor general's report it appeared that there were 10,384 employees in the year ended March 31, 1944, and the total expenditure was $5 million odd as indicated in my statement, and he asked for an explanation as to why that figure should be nearly double the number indicated for the current year. I had not had an opportunity of checking it at that time but I indicated that I thought in all probability the explanation was that hourlyrated employees were not included in the total number indicated in the auditor general's report, and that is the case. The total number of employees in the year ended 1944 was 10,384 made up as follows:	5,586 hourly
rated employees, which would be ordinary labour and the like, and 4,798 coming under the civil service commission, or a total of 10,384, and the remuneration of the 5,586 hourly paid employees would be distributed in different items principally under the heading, I believe, No. 10, repair and upkeep of ships and the like. But my hon. friend was quite right that the statement as it appeared in the auditor general's report might be misleading in view of the figures I had given the night before.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I wonder whether the
minister has given the committee all the information he can with regard to the question I raised when I asked that he report on what I understood to be the recruiting campaign. He has indicated that he does not look upon it as a recruiting compaign, and he has given certain figures, but one of my questions was, what offer is being made to those who may remain in the service in this two-year force, as regards pay and allowances.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I had already stated what
I thought the terms and conditions were as to pay and allowances with respect to the interim force so called; that is to say, they are exactly the same as are now being received by hostilities-only personnel-the active service rates of pay and allowances. In my statement with respect to the army. I pointed out-and the statement applied to all three services-that a committee had been set up to review the question of the permanent rates
of pay, I gave an undertaking that this would be announced not later than March 31 next, and that when it was announced those who had joined the interim force would have the right to go into the so-called permanent force at rates of pay and allowances, whatever they are, for that force, and should they not wish to avail themselves of that right they would be relieved of their undertaking to serve until September 30, 1947. But so long as they serve in the interim force, so called, their rates of pay and allowances will be those which they are now receiving. So the man who goes into the interim force knows, from the dollar point of view, what he is going to get. He does not know yet, if he is going to stay on in the permanent force, what the permanent rates will be, but we have told him that he will know that before March 31, and he has only to wait that comparatively short period before he is in a position to decide whether he wants to stay in or not. I am sorry I cannot give more definite information on that question yet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am still a little confused about this. In the original statement the minister said he anticipated getting this balance figure, which is about 6,000 from three sources: new enlistments, people transferring, and cadets. I do not think the minister has given information in regard to those coming in fresh, new raw recruits, shall we call them. In the original statement, to which more than one member has referred, which appeared in the press, it was said that something like seventy per cent of those that were coming forward were new recruits.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is completely incorrect. I d/o not know where that figure came from. We are not taking in new recruits at the moment. If some specially attractive lad came along I do not say that we might not take him, because the establishment is there; but speaking from memory, I believe that since last June we have taken very few new recruits into the navy. With 95,000 on strength, we felt that was the peak, and up to the present that applies so far as enlistments for the post-war navy are concerned. Naturally we shall be resuming at some time in the not distant future the enlistment of new recruits, but so far we have neither sought nor encouraged the entry of new recruits. As yet we are looking to men who are presently serving or have recently served.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I desire to direct a question to the minister having in mind the answers which were brought down on page 609 of Hansard of October 1, 1945. These
Dfmobilizalion-Naval Services

questions were answered at the instance of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and they related to personnel recently appointed by the Department of Veterans Affairs. I take it that between the two departments of government there is a close liaison where matters affect the naval services. I wish to bring this to the attention Of the minister. The question was in three parts:
1.	How many persons have been appointed to positions in the Department of Veterans Affairs since its inception in 1944?
2.	How many positions have been established where the official concerned is in receipt of $3,600 per annum or more?
3.	What was the previous army, navy or air force rank held by such persons holding these' positions?
The question boiled down to its smallest proportions means that perhaps the more important positions relating to these appointments were of course asked for in the second part of the question, namely, how many positions have been established where the official concerned is in receipt of $3,600 per annum or more. Now, the strange part of the answer, it seems to me, and one which I think the minister ought to have concerned himself with when these appointments were made is this- perhaps as a newcomer to the department we should not place upon his shoulders a responsibility that is not his. I think he should watch these matters, because of all those appointed to positions in the Department of Veterans Affairs since its inception in 1944 the navy has not got a single one.
The naval service of this country deserves something better than that. There were eighty-seven appointments from the army and seventeen from the air force. I am not making any reflection upon that proportion or upon the appointment of any one of these men. but I do criticize the government for allowing the appointments to be made without having some representation from the naval service, w'hich has done an . excellent job in this war. A fairly substantial number of naval personnel is involved in the rehabilitation programme of the government and the country. It does seem to me that there has been a strange and serious default on the part of the government in that the navy seems to have been forgotten or neglected in the appointment of men to key positions in the new department. Have any representations been made to the minister by his department in that connection? If not, will the minister see that this oversight is corrected at the earliest possible moment? The navy, being fMr. Graydon.]
one of the great branches of our armed forces, ought to be given more consideration than zero in appointments made since 1944.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am grateful to my hon. friend for bringing this to my attention. The first information I would have to seek, of course, would be to find out if any naval personnel had applied for these positions. The hon: member knows as wmll as I do that the appointments are made by the civil service commission. They are advertised; they are open to everyone. I agree with him it is unusual to find that in such a very large list, naval personnel should not be included. I shall ask our personnel people if they have had any inquiries about it. Probably the answer is that for one reason or another no naval personnel have applied. I feel safe in saying there has been no discrimination in the Department of Veterans Affairs so far as naval personnel are concerned. In view of what my hon. friend has said the only question that arises in my mind is whether or not we ought to suggest to my colleague, the Minister of Veterans Affairs, that a special effort be made to get some naval veterans to apply so that he will have that representation in his department. I should be very sorry if there were intentional discrimination against the naval service, and I am sure there has not been. I am obliged to the hon. member for bringing it to my attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The minister said a few minutes ago that there had been no recruits taken into the navy since June.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: So far as I know, from the general public.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I believe there were some lads taken in in Ma3' and June.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That may be; I was speaking from memory as to the date.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I would ask him to explain what is being done with these young men. I know of some who were taken in about that time and received perhaps two or three weeks' training. Ever since then they have been kept kicking around barracks in one or other of the larger cities in Canada. They are not receiving .even physical training,-and certainly no naval training. Some of those lads signed \ip in the permanent navy for seven years. It is a very poor way to start a young man out. He goes into the navy full of enthusiasm; he wants to make it his life work, and yet he is just being pushed from pillar to post. I realize that the navy has been busy on demobilization and many other things, but it is a great tragedy that these young men should not be given proper training right now. There

Demobilization-Naval Services
are also some of these young men who joined up oniy for the period of the war. They 'cannot be demobilized because they came in such a short time ago. I believe that they too are being kicked around and that no training is being carried on for them. There is no better way to break the morale of a high-spirited young man than by such a process. The minister may be unaware that this has been going on. If he is, I do wish he would check up right away, because I think he will agree with me that it is an unsatisfactory state of affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend that it is most unsatisfactory. I was not aware that that' was the case. I find it a little surprising, because at our big training schools, for instance at Cornwallis in Nova Scotia, we. are continuing the training of men who come in early in the year. I think our last class will graduate there about November 1; therefore I find it hard to understand why those who came in in May or June, as my hon. friend suggested, should be left, as he puts it, kicking around in the division doing nothing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I did not. say they are doing nothing; they are probably running messages and scrubbing floors or doing other jobs of that type, but they are not getting any training.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Even that surprises me, because, as I say, we are still maintaining our training establishment at Cornwallis to complete the training of those who have come in earlier in the year. However, I shall most certainly make inquiries as to the circumstances to which my hon. friend alludes, and if he can give me some further particulars later to enable me to pursue it more quickly, I shall be very grateful.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is any training school in operation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: At Cornwallis.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is it to be carried on after this course finishes?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Not for the time being. We are closing Cornwallis because it is obviously too big to operate in peace time. Other "arrangements will have to be made. St. Hyacinthe is still operating the signal school. Of course it is quite possible to carry out basic training of recruits in divisions, and then they would be sent either to the east or to the west coast for continued training there. Up to the present the main training has been carried on at Cornwallis for ordinary ratings and at St. Hyacinthe for signals. Both are still operating.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Are there any training facilities in Canada that can be put to use on a small scale to train these young men?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Oh, yes, on either coast.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Would it not be possible to carry on training at Cornwallis on a smaller scale?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Quite. There is no lack of training facilities and no intention that the training of partly trained personnel should not be continued.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
There is one thing
troubling me; perhaps the minister can explain it. The low-point men at present in the navy come up for discharge in their turn; if he is not accepting new recruits for the navy now, and if he has not a trained force of new men, coming forward all the time, how is he going to keep the ships of the navy manned until such time as he starts his new recruiting campaign and brings the navy up to its full strength?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: As I say, we are not accepting new recruits. That is a very short term policy, if I might put it that way. I think I indicated last night that at the moment we hope to get the bulk of the men to hold our navy, shall we say, at a strength, as I indicated, of around ten thousand, from those who have already had a fairly complete and expensive training from the country. If too many of those wrant to go back to civil life, do not want to continue in the navy, then of course we shall have to build it up from new men who have had no training at all. In any case we will resume very soon the taking on of new enlistments from the sea cadets and from the general public. I think it is probably fair to say that, as was indicated by the hon. member for Churchill last night, a great many of those who served even one or two 'years ma,y not want to continue on in the navy. I am not suggesting we are going to be able to carry on our navy for more than a few' months by enlisting only those who have already served for a time in this war. I do not want the committee or the country to get the impression that recruiting for the navy is suspended indefinitely. I suggest that it may only be, and probably will only be, for a month or two.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I should like to know how many officers are employed at naval headquarters and at local district headquarters, with their ranks, and at the same time I should like to know if there has been any reduction in these figures since V-E day; if so, what is the reduction?
Demobilization-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot give the ranks; I can give the totals, and I could get a break-down of the ranks a little later. First dealing with naval service headquarters, at August 17, 1945, V-J day, there were employed 667 officers and 1,102 ratings, a total of 1,769. As of October 22, 1945, there were employed a total of 497 officers, a reduction of 170, and a total of 915 ratings, a reduction of 1S7, making a grand total of 1,412 or a total reduction of 357. I have not as yet the information for the divisions, but my hon. friend indicated that he might ask this ques-. tion and probably I will have that information later this afternoon.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
What is the
lowest ranking officer in the navy who can impose a sentence of thirty-four days' stoppage of pay?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am afraid I shall have to get that information and give it to my hon. friend a little later on. I am not as up to date on matters of discipline as perhaps I should be.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Could the minister tell me offhand whether an officer with the rank of lieutenant is able to impose that fine?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No, I am afraid I cannot. I will make inquiries and let my hon. friend know a little later.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am sorry to take up time on this matter, but to my mind it is a very important question. Yesterday there was some question raised as to whether or not Nelson was dead. From some things we see and hear I believe he Is still living, and in some wrays I am not at all sorry. I have occasion at the present time, however, to be working on a case in which I am personally interested, because it is from my home town. I have found that a penalty has been imposed by a naval officer in the women's division with the rank of lieutenant, amounting to thirty-four days' stoppage of pay; and it was imposed upon a Wren who has given twenty-six months' service. The family from which she comes has a total of seven on active service in this war, and I am afraid this is an ignoble ending for her. If such are the regulations in the navy, I think we should look up that Nelson affair and see if we cannot bring it to light. I should be very glad to have this information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I would not like to have that statement pass without referring to it briefly. I am familiar with the case to which

my hon. friend refers. He was good enough to tell me about it, and I looked into it. Whether or not the officer who imposed the penalty was qualified to do so I am not prepared to say; I will make inquiries, but from the information given me I should say the penalty imposed was not excessive. After all the navy, like any other service, has certain standards of discipline which it must maintain.
I would not be prepared to say, after looking into the matter, that the officer who imposed that penalty exceeded her jurisdiction or that the penalty was excessive.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I cannot speak from the naval point of view, but from the point of view of the army, in which I have had considerable experience, I should say the penalty was very excessive. It was imposed for being absent without leave for seven days, and that absence was under very extenuating circumstances. This girl's husband had been discharged from the Uganda, and she applied for leave. She w'as given forty-eight hours' leave. She overstayed seven days and came back, and now is finishing Her career in the navy with thirty-four days' stoppage of pay.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: My hon. friend should add that previously she had been given three weeks' sleeping out passes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Speaking from the army point of view, sleeping out passes do not mean very much. You do all your work in the daytime and you are your own boss at night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Would the minister say whether any naval service personnel are being used in the army of occupation in Germany?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Have there been any requests on the part of any naval service personnel to serve there? Perhaps the minister for air would say whether the air force is serving in that army of occupation to a comparable extent with the army. I believe we have a few squadrons there, but I should like to know whether the army is bearing the whole brunt of this service in Germany.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
We have had no requests to [DOT] serve in the army of occupation, and no naval service personnel are so serving. I do not know whether my hon. friend the minister for air cares to answer for his department. That question perhaps should be.asked when his own estimates are under consideration, but we might be able to dispose of it now.

Demobilization-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We have supplied the squadrons that have been requested for the occupational force, and they are still serving.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: At the same time I do not want this to be taken as a precedent so that we may cover the whole waterfront as far as questions are concerned. We are on the naval estimates now, and I beg the committee to stick to questions relating to the navy and to the items under discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
A few
moments ago the minister stated that the Cornwallis training station would be closed November 1.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No, I said our last class would graduate on November 1. Perhaps I misled my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Then I
understood the minister to say further that Cornwallis was too large for any peace-time use by the navy. I should like to ask what disposition it is expected will be made of that establishment, which cost this country an enormous sum. A return brought down October 1 stated that the total expenditure there was $9,163,643.63. In a previous session I understood that it would continue to be used as a training centre, at least to some extent, to do the work carried on in earlier years in Nova Scotia by the naval college, which was demolished in 1917 at the time of the explosion. Is the minister in a position to make a statement now? If not, I should like him to do so at a convenient time later.
Mr. ABBOTT; I think perhaps I can make the statement now. As far as the navy is concerned, Cornwallis is far too large for any possible post-war use. It was built for a very special purpose. There was an urgent need to train seamen at a critical time during the war, and Cornwallis was built and equipped to perform that work, which was splendidly done. Various possibilities now are being explored with other government departments as to uses which might be matle of Cornwallis. If it could be used as a rehabilitation centre or training centre or something of the sort, the navy perhaps could utilize a portion of it for training purposes; but as a centre it is larger than the navy could possibly contemplate or maintain in peace time. So if no other use is found for it, as far as the navy is concerned we would contemplate relinquishing it about the end of the present fiscal year. Beyond that I cannot say. If it followed the ordinary course; if no other use were found, it would be declared surplus by the navy and
its ultimate disposition then would be handed over to some other government department, the crown assets allocation committee, for instance. I can say that various possibilities are now being actively explored.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
There is a large hospital structure at the Cornwallis naval station, which was built and equipped at heavy expense. What use is being made of it now, and what will be the final disposition of it?
Mr. ABBOTT; In addition to completing the training of certain ratings, as I mentioned, Cornwallis is being used as a demobilization centre. It is admirably suited for that purpose. The hospital facilities are being utilized for the examination of men who are being discharged. When that work is completed, the hospital as well as the other facilities at Cornwallis will be declared surplus by the navy. When that time comes my responsibility as Minister of National Defence for Naval Services will cease so far as Cornwallis is concerned. I cannot tell my hon. friend what will be done with the hospital or the other facilities, but the navy will be finished with them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I received a telegram
yesterday asking if the good name of the ships' company of H.M.C.S. Uganda might be vindicated because of the slurring remarks that have been made regarding some of the men who had not volunteered for service in the Pacific. Is' it correct that all the men of the ship's company of the Uganda originally volunteered for service wherever required, and that later the government gave them the opportunity of volunteering or not for the Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows
as well as I, the men on the Uganda volun- . teered to serve anywhere. After the termination of the European war, and in accordance with the announced government policy, those men, as well as the men in the army and in the air force, were offered the opportunity of electing whether or not they would continue to serve in the Pacific. I received a wire similar to the one received by my hon. friend, and I am replying that I feel sure that the majority of the people of this country are under no illusions as to the status of the crew of the Uganda or as to their suffering from any alleged slurs which may have been cast with respect to their terms of service.

Demobilization-Naval Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I should like to ask a
question with regard to the service of certain officers who served with the Royal Canadian Navy in the last war and who rejoined the navy in this war. These men were straight stripe officers, and many of them served in senior executive positions. Is there any differential between the pay and allowances of the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, that is, between the straight navy and the wavy navy? Is there any difference in the pension facilities offered to the officers in the two services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Answering the first question, there is no distinction in pay as between the two branches of the service. As the hon. member has indicated, a number of former Royal Canadian Navy officers rejoined the navy at the beginning of this war. As a matter of fact they have performed outstanding services. Their pay and allowances have been the same as those of the officers of the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve. As to pensions, I am advised that if these men rejoined the navy their service during the war would count on their pensions. For instance, if they had left the navy prior to this war before reaching pensionable age and rejoined the navy at the beginning of this war, their previous service plus their service in this war would count toward pension. I take it that these men have come back as reserve officers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is a question several of them have been asking.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What is the relationship between the merchant marine and the navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
There is none at all. We
provided guns and naval gunners for merchant marine ships, but we have nothing to do with them now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What are the amounts to be voted for civil salaries and pay and allowances for H.M.C.S. Queen of Regina for 1945-46?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The estimates are not
broken down in that way, but if my hon. friend wishes that information I can [DOT]see that it is obtained and given to him later on. He wants the actual expenditures in connection with H.M.C.S. Queen in the previous year?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I want the proposed expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: For this year?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That may be rather difficult to get broken down in that way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: You have a civil list covering H.M.C.S. Queen.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
There would be rent and
maintenance and all that sort of thing. I think I can probably give my hon. friend a fairly accurate figure of what the total estimates would include for H.M.C.S. Queen.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
What is the proposed future
of H.M.C.S. Queen.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I think I can give an answer with respect to all divisions. As I indicated in my opening remarks, we propose to maintain all divisions, but as to the scale on which they will be maintained and other matters, I am not yet in position to make a definite announcement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
How many admirals,
vice admirals, rear admirals and captains are there on the strength of the navy to-day, and what will the policy be with regard to bringing them down to peace-time strength? A great many of them are permanent force people.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I shall have to get that
information and give it to my hon. friend later.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Is the minister able to give
us any information about the ships that are manned at the present time? For example, I presume the Uganda no longer has a crew large enough to take her to sea. Are many of these naval ships to be tied up until the permanent navy is organized to a greater degree than it is at the present time, or is an attempt to be made to keep a certain number of ships active throughout the year? Just what is the plan?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I think I can answer that
in a fairly general way by saying that the Uganda is refitting at Esquimalt and-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Has the Uganda a crew large enough to put to sea?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Yes, we have more than
enough men. The position is that a great many men who would normally be assigned to the Uganda are now being used to destore a large number of ships, such as corvettes, frigates and that sort of thing. During the transition period which will last for two or three months we will need a great many trained naval personnel, particularly stokers and that sort of thing, for destoring and winterizing purposes. There is a heavy programme of so-called winterizing, that is, making ships safe for the winter.
I am not making this as a definite statement, but the present plans are that the Uganda will sail before the end of the year to go around through the Panama canal on a training

Demobilization-Naval Services
cruise with a certain number of new men who are now on her, cadet officers and that sort of thing. As I announced the other day, the Ontario will be back at Esquimalt, I think in about a month. She will presumably have to go into dock for a refit. It is not expected that during the winter we will keep two cruisers cruising about. There is no war on, and it would entail considerable extra expense for fuel and that sort of thing to keep them at sea. We do not contemplate keeping both the Uganda and the Ontario at sea during the winter. The committee knows that in broad terms our strength at the moment is roughly
5,000	permanent men, and there are still a large number of hostilities-only personnel. We want to bring those down to the minimum before February or March. Our plan is that as we reduce the hostilities personnel we shall build up with interim or permanent force men to take their place. The present plans are that the Uganda will leave Esquimalt certainly before the end of the year on a cruise, as I have indicated.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The cruisers will be based in Canada, not in far eastern waters.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Their home base will be Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We have no commitments in the far east such as to put down piracy, and so forth?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We have had no request for that sort of thing. I would hope that these new and modern ships we are getting would make cruises to different parts of the world, to the far east and elsewhere. That is far more interesting to the crews than to be tied up to the jetty or to be cruising up and down our own coasts. I have every expectation that they will have cruises, but just when they will start it is a little early for me to say.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It will make the navy a lot .more popular.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am sure it would.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: You have sold all the corvettes and all the Fairmiles. There are none available?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The navy does not sell them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
In some eases it would look as if we were giving them away.
turned over to crown assets allocation committee, which in turn presumably turns them over to War Assets Corporation, which has been set up as an agency to dispose of what is surplus. I can answer no questions with respect to the disposal of anything by War Assets Corporation. I have nothing to do with the price or the method of disposal. It is not my responsibility.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: But the minister has to ask parliament for the money for the navy. He does not know how the ships are disposed of or what they bring?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The navy does not get the money; it goes to consolidated revenue. The navy comes to the house every year for a vote.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that all the corvettes and Fairmiles have been disposed of?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: They have all been declared surplus so far as the navy is concerned. I do not know whether War Assets has disposed of them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There was a statement in the press last night that they had.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I saw that. As I explained in my preliminary remarks, they are not the type of ship that we feel are suitable for the permanent post-war navy. They were built for a special purpose, to do a special job, and so far as the navy is concerned our future plans do not contemplate retaining them. We are keeping a certain number of frigates in reserve and for training purposes. They are a larger and more modern ship. But the corvettes and Fairmiles-no. With two or three isolated exceptions, they are all surplus, and so far as I know they are being disposed of.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Are you not keeping some of the minesweepers of the newer class for training purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It has not definitely been decided yet. We have some of the Algerines and some minesweepers in reserve.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Will personnel of the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve be permitted to take part in some of the cruises which have been indicated, on the Uganda, for instance? When will the cruises commence?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I would appreciate it if my Mr. ABBOTT: I am not in a position to hon. friend would stick to the naval depart-	indicate any definite date, but I	hope that itment. When the navy is through with any	will be possible by next spring.	Our plan atship, it declares it surplus. It has nothing to do present is to reduce the hostilities personnel with selling it. With two or three isolated	and to take in new men to build	up our navyexceptions, all our corvettes and Fairmiles	to its post-war complement, and	at the same
have been declared surplus and have been time there will be active training of the 47696-97



Demobilization-Naval Services
reserve. I would hope that early next year, probably next spring or summer, we shall be able to carry out training for the reserve on board ship, but I am not in a position to make any announcement now. I would have to discuss it with the staff and see how they felt.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
There are now about
5,000	personnel in the permanent force?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The permanent force has about 4,000, and 1,100 have applied for interim two-year service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The 1945-46 estimate for pay and allowances is $98,351,247, and in the minister's statement the other night of naval expenditures for 1944-45 I noticed that the estimate made at the beginning of the year almost exactly equalled the expenditure for the year. That is pretty good figuring when dealing with figures of such magnitude. I would like the assurance from the minister at this time, because this money is voted by the house, that it will not necessarily be spent if a saving of the taxpayers' money can be saved. In other words, men will not be retained in the service just in order to spend this money?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I will most certainly give that assurance. The estimate for pay and allowances last year was $114,000,000 odd, and the actual expenditures were $123,000,000 odd.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I was taking the whole estimate.
, Mr. ABBOTT: I was referring to pay and allowances. The estimate for this year is $98,000,000, or a reduction from last year's expenditure of some $24,000,000. As my hon. friend will appreciate, these estimates are made up on the best guess the staff can make as to the average number of man-hours that will be served in the navy from-April 1, 1945 to March 31, 1946. If demobilization proceeds more rapidly than we anticipated, this estimated figure will be cut down. I can assure my hon. friend that every effort will be made to keep it down as low as possible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There would be senior officers on the staff that you would not be justified in retaining with a cutting down of personnel.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The minister said a moment ago that these estimates are made up on the best guess the department can make.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It is bound to be a guess, but with informed knowledge.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: -There is no accurate yardstick which they can use?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The estimating is pretty good, if my hon. friend will compare the estimate last year and the actual expenditure. I have been astounded at the accuracy with which the accounting staffs can estimate.
Mr. CASE; No, the minister said they guess.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Perhaps "guess" is a slur on their abilities in estimating accurately, but there must be a certain element of guesswork in it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am surprised that the hon. member for Grey North should be surprised at a guess from the government benches.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: If the minister has so much confidence in his guess, I suggest the government might very well have brought down this whple appropriation of $1,365,000,000 in three or four hundred different resolutions, the way he does with his ordinary estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: In order that we might learn just where the increases are in the actual expenditure and the estimates, would the minister give a break-down of both into, I suggest, about six classes. First, pay: then, the assigned pay; dependents' allowance; uniform allowance; allowance in lieu of quarters and rations, and clothing on discharge. By getting a break-down of the estimates and of the actual expenditures we may find where this increase of $8,600,000 has taken place.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am advised that to get information in the form and detail for which my hon. friend has asked would require the services of a considerable accounting staff for some time. But a short explanation of the increase, I am informed, is that the major portion of the increase is the amount of twenty-nine cents per man which represented the additional number that had to be placed out on lodging and compensation and could not be accommodated in barracks. In the estimates for the previous year allowance was not made for that factor. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I know of a number of lads coming back to Ontario. I do not know whether they were on leave or were being sent back, but in any event they were returning after serving on our ships in the Aleutians, and I presume the intention of the department was that they should have the best possible transportation back. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: My hon. friend is as familiar as I am with the problems under which the railways have been operating during the war. During every holiday season the railway companies, I thought, cooperated by seeing that the service personnel were allowed if possible to get on the trains before civilians, but it was not possible to run special trains for service personnel, so far as I know. They had to take their chance with the others, but by and large the transportation facilities of Canada have stood up wonderfully and I have not heard any serious complaints from service personnel that they were unable to get accommodation to reach their homes. Some had to stand up, it is true, and so did some of the rest of us, but that wras all right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The minister has not satisfied me of the justification for

Demobilization-Naval Services
the increase in the estimates for transportation for the navy for the current fiscal year. It is the only one of the three defence departments for which an increase is asked, and that increase amounts to about $300,000. The army is asking in its estimates for a reduction of about thirty per cent and the air services for a reduction of about thirteen per cent, but the naval department is asking for an increase. There would be no expenditures for transportation for navy men, or to a very limited extent at any rate, on the water. I do not think we have had sufficient justification for this increase, and I would like to have a further explanation from the minister. Will he tell us why there should be an increase in the cost of transportation for the naval department while there is a reduction, and it is a reasonable reduction, of thirty per cent for the army and thirteen per cent for the air services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I do not know that I can offer much more explanation than I have given. One factor to which I have not referred is the fact that the strength of the navy was increased this year. Last year the estimates were based on a total strength of
87.000	and this year the peak strength was 95,000, nearly 9,000 more. Every one of those
95.000	will travel at least once in reaching his home during the year. The actual expenditures for transportation for the six months up to September 30 was about forty-seven per cent of the estimates. It was $4,662,919, leaving a balance of about $5 million. That would indicate perhaps that the estimate was sufficiently conservative and that it would probably not be reached; but it was made up in the same way that the estimates for pay and allowances were made up, on the average number of men in the army, and the per capita rate. The per capita rate in 1944-45 was $101, and this year we are estimating seven-twelfths of that, which would be $59, plus $6 to provide for increased transportation costs due to demobilization. That "is only an estimate. The [DOT] expenditures for the previous year were $101 per man. This year we are taking seven-twelfths of that and adding $6 to cover additional cost of transportation by reason of demobilization. What the result will be remains to be seen, but the actual result for the first six months is forty-seven per cent of the estimated expenditures.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Could we have a better
break-down of this item? According to page

Demobilization-Naval Services
550 of Hansard it amounts to $14,908,124, and in the mimeographed copy that we received showing the comparison of estimates for this year and last year it is broken down to show capital expenditures, repairs,- operating expenses and rentals. Could we have it further broken down to show the amounts for construction, purchase of property, repairs, operating expenses and for rentals? Then would the minister tell us what construction has been done this year; where it was done; who did it and what it cost, in each instance? Would he tell us also if it is the intention to carry on further construction projects this year, and if so, where will they be -carried on, and, if they are to be carried on, could he give us some idea of the nature of the work proposed to be done? I would also ask if it is the intention to purchase further properties this year out of this money that is being voted and, if so, where those properties are located, from whom they are to be purchased and what amounts are to be paid for them. As to the item for rentals, would he give us particulars about them, what rentals are being paid, where and to whom; and how does the amount compare with the amounts paid in rentals last year?	,

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to give that information. As rtiy hon. friend will appreciate, some of what he has asked is a pretty tall order. We have a great many rented properties across the country for which various rentals are paid, with various persons from whom they are rented. Of course I could not be expected to give that detail to the committee to-day, but perhaps I might make a general statement on this question of property and maintenance. Then I will look at my hon. friend's remarks in Hansard and endeavour to get the information for which he has asked.
First on the matter of capital expenditures, by the end of the fiscal year 1943-44 capital expenditure on shore buildings and properties for the navy had reached its peak. During that year and the preceding year a total of over S50,000,000 was spent on this item. As the requirements diminished, the expenditures also decreased; but the actual .payment of accounts lagged considerably behind the completion of the projects. Although some construction was completed in the year 1944-45, this was to a large extent a liquidating period. Of the total amount requested for this fiscal year, that is to say $7,017,590, we have already spent practically $2,000,000 to close accounts from 1944-45, and as of August 31 there still remained an unpaid liability for work commenced or under contract in 1944-45 amounting to nearly $3,000,000, which means that in this
year we have had to provide roughly $5,000,000 out of a total of some $7,000,000 to meet the ' costs of construction started in other years. The balance requested, of slightly over $2,000,000, represents the cost of projects commenced in 1945-46 including those which are essential for demobilization and posthostility activities of the Royal Canadian Navy, and temporary repairs to the Bedford magazines. The balance may be considered as cash needed for 1945-46 projects to March 31, 1946, being composed of the actual payments to August 31, plus estimated payments possible by March 31, 1946. The actual amount required for reconstruction of the .Bedford magazines cannot be determined until Colonel Ogilvie's report on the whole situation has been reviewed carefully and the necessary calculations made.
To summarize the way the item of $7,017,590 is made up, therefore, first we have the carry-over from 1944-45 as of August 31, 1945, amounting to $2,809,103. Then we have expenditures to August 31, 1945, of $2,091,091, and provision for 1945A6 projects, $2,117,396, making the total of $7,017,590.
The principal items in respect of which provision is made in the amount of $2,117,396, which is the amount we are estimating as still to be spent, are as follows: Halifax, $450,000: crane for wharf No. 4; retaining walls and wharf repairs; steam supply lines; miscellaneous buildings; fifty-ton hammerhead crane for Dartmouth and temporary repairs to Bedford magazines. Renous, $540,000: maintenance workshop; boiler house; empty package storehouse; ten magazines; traverses around magazines. I shall have a word to say about that in a moment. These are estimates. Esquimalt, $200,000: motor transport shop; empty package storehouse; road repairs; dockyard. Kamloops, $664,000: empty package storehouse; twrelve magazines; traverses around magazines; services-water, steam, electrical, sewage. Sydney, $213,000: construction of stores building; railway sidings; empty package store. Miscellaneous requirements, including radio stations, $70,396. This makes up the total of $2,117,396. That, I may say, will be subject to some substantial reduction by reason of a reduction in the magazine requirements at Renous and Kamloops, which follow the end of the war and rearrangement of our magazine requirements.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The minister mentioned the crane on wharf No. 4 in Halifax. Does that wharf belong to the Halifax harbour commission or does it belong to the dominion government?
Demobilization-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am advised that the wharf belongs to the navy; it is in the dock yard. As to the second part of my hon. friend's question, relating to the provision for repairs, operating expenses and rentals, the total estimated provision for the current year is $7,890,534, of which actual expenditures for the first six months amounted to $3,037,819 or about 38 per cent. The total amount estimated represents an increase over the estimated expenses of last year but is approximately the same as the actual expenses, a difference of some $14,000. The item includes provision for rental of properties; services, water, electricity and the like; fuel for heating; repairs and maintenance of buildings; alterations and repairs to machinery. There is an increase in the estimated provision of $1,174,643 over the provision made last year, but as I indicated a moment ago the decrease from the actual amount expended is only $14,841. The estimated increase is explained largely by the fact that as the building programme of the navy comes to a conclusion, the cost of maintenance increases. Another contributing factor is that, as I indicated yesterday, civilian personnel will replace naval personnel in maintenance and repair work. This will continue to be the case until such time as the buildings which are at present occupied, and which will continue to be occupied until the end of the present fiscal year, are declared surplus to requirements and disposed of through the crown assets allocation committee or the War Assets Corporation. Steps have been taken already to give up all rented premises which are not essential, and it is anticipated that by March 31, 1946, only a few rented properties will not have been returned to their owners. I have not the details here as to the properties which we now rent, the individual rentals and the persons from whom rented. I will obtain that and give it to my hon. friend a little later.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The minister did not answer my question as to what construction had been done this year, who had done it, where it was done and what it had cost. I also asked what repairs had been made this year, where they were made, who made them and what they had cost.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The hon. member will realize that it would be practically impossible to give him that information without referring to data other than what I have before me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Would questions about H.M.C.S. York come under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Yes.
[Mr. HazeD 1

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Details as to that ship were not included in the information given.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That would be a completion of last year's contract. I was giving the particulars of $2,000,000 odd of contracts which are being undertaken this year. H. M. C. S. York would come under the other item of $5,000,000 covering the completion of last year's contracts.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
What percentage of
civilian personnel is employed at the Halifax dockyards?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That alters from day to day. I have not the information here, but I shall try to get the latest figure and give it to my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Why should civilian personnel be employed at a naval dockyard? Why should not all employees be subject to naval discipline?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: To all intents and purposes a naval dockyard is an industrial establishment. There is no reason for employing a man in uniform to cut pipe or to do ordinary industrial operations in a dockyard. As I indicated the other night, it was necessary to do that during war time in order to assure that the men would be there and be subject to naval discipline, but strictly speaking they are not sailors. They are civilian workers doing a civilian job and they should be working as civilians. As my hon. friend will realize, from the long term point of view it is not desirable to employ service personnel in purely civilian work, because the service personnel are given special privileges in the nature of pensions and that sort of thing which are not available to their opposite numbers doing the same jobs in civilian life.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Under whose supervision is the refitting of these ships completed? I am not so sure that, now that the war is over, there is not quite a bit of loafing on the job at some of the naval dockyards. They are in no hurry to complete the refitting, because in some cases it is not intended to send the ship to sea. I am concerned over the fact that it is quite possible we are, paying tradesmen rates of $1.25 an hour to just loaf on the job. I would ask the minister to look into this matter and make sure that it is not happening on a large scale.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I will take note of my hon. friend's remarks.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I have no
specific details, but it has been brought to my

Demobilization-Naval Services
attention that large expenditures have recently been made, and perhaps are still being made, in connection with repairs and overhaul of naval vessels which have been or are to be declared surplus. If this complaint is not correct, it certainly should be denied or explained by the minister.
Will the minister include in his statement of expenditures for construction at these naval stations the details of expenditures at Cornwallis Naval Station, which he stated is to be abandoned. Some time ago I asked questions with regard to the cost of coal, freight and demurrage on purchases of coal for the Cornwallis station, and replies are to be found on page 602 of Hansard of October 1. It was reported that large outlays for demurrage had been made in connection with shipments of United States coal. One of my questions was:
What was the cost per ton, the freight, demurrage, commission and total cost of each purchase?
The answer in connection with demurrage was as follows:
First forty-eight hours, free; next twenty-four hours, $1 per car per day; next twenty-four hours, $1 per car per day; each twenty-four hours thereafter, $5 per car per day.
Some people might say that that was "a fast one" when that reply was brought down, but I would not accuse the minister of that because that is not his method. I do not presume he can do so to-day, but at a later date I should like him to give the total cost of demurrage on coal supplied to the Corn-' wallis naval station, from whom that coal was purchased and where it was shipped from.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows,
all purchases of coal and like supplies are made by the Department of Munitions and Supply. The return which he got was made by that department, not by the naval department.
The other question as to what work is being done on ships would properly come under another item, but I shall answer it now. The inference is being left that a lot of unnecessary work is being done on ships. Some ships were in dockyard being refitted when V-J day came along. Some of these ships were being reconverted for the Pacific, and we had to decide whether the work should be entirely abandoned or whether it should be completed. The works had been pulled out of many of the ships and, if they were ever going to be used, something had to be done. We arrived at the decision that, where the work was approximately ninety per cent completed, it would be completed. Other work that was being done in the dockyards was what we 47696-98
described as winterizing of ships. That consists of draining the water out of the pipes and getting them in shape so that they can be laid up. That work is being done on frigates, corvettes and other ships which are being turned over to War Assets Corporation for disposal. I can assure the committee that there is no unnecessary work being done on ships which are being declared surplus. Any work that is being done is solely to conserve their value or to make them more valuable on disposal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is it the intention of the naval department to use the building on Cartier square as headquarters for the navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
It is for the time being,
but I do not know how long that will continue. I can assure my hon. friend that it will continue to be used up to the end of the present fiscal year, and probably some time after.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The minister indicated
that where ninety per cent of the work had been done on a ship, it was completed. What was the position with regard to vessels, on which eighty per cent, sixty per cent and fifty per cent of the work had been done? In many cases the entrails of the vessels would have been removed and placed on the quay, and the vessel towed away.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It was felt that for disposal purposes they would fetch just as much in that condition as if a substantial additional amount were paid to refit them. The best advice I could get was that it would not pay to continue the work on a ship that was less than about ninety per cent completed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Then they had to be towed to some place for disposal; for they could not steam there themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Most of them would be towed. The hon. member for York South asked as to the number of officers in the divisions. The total number is 821.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is that officers or all ranks?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Officers. The figure 821 is made up as follows: Tbronto, 211; Winnipeg, 55; Halifax, 5; Edmonton, 20; Hamilton, 34; Saint John, N.B., 53; Vancouver, 43; Windsor, 24; London, 23; Ottawa, 20; Montreal, 177; Esquimalt, 3; Regina, 16; Kingston, 20; Port Arthur, 17; Quebec, 47; Charlottetown, 12; Calgary, 20, and Saskatoon, 21.
During the past two months divisions at Quebec, Montreal. Toronto and Saint John, New Brunswick, in addition to the normal functions of a naval division, bear for pay the

Demobilization-Naval Services

staffs of the naval officers in charge at these ports. These staffs represent approximately 200 officers. There are also 100 counsellor officers and thirty rehabilitation officers borne for demobilization duties at the naval divisions. These 330 officers are included in the figure of 821 shown above.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I would judge that the figures include chief petty officers and other non-commissioned ranks. There are certainly not thirty-four commissioned officers in Hamilton. I know there are not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: These are the figures I was given. They probably include warrant officers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: They must include chief petty officers, too. They are not necessarily all warrant officers, are they?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: How many naval stations are there such as Cornwallis, St. Hyacinthe and Royal Roads? Is the same policy being applied to all these schools as the minister informed the committee is being applied to Cornwallis? The minister said that Cornwallis naval station is to be completely closed at the end of this fiscal year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Royal Roads, as my hon. friend knows, is the naval college. Cornwallis was established for training naval ratings. St. Hyacinthe was the school at which signalling instruction was given. Those were the three principal schools outside of Halifax and Esquimait.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Were there any others?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There were no other establishments during the war with the exception that officers training was carried on at King's college in Halifax, Nova Scotia. Subsequently to the closing of these war-time establishments instruction of ratings will be carried on at the main naval bases at Halifax and Esquimait.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Cornwallis and St. Hyacinthe will both be closed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is my present information. They are both large war-time schools.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What others will be closed?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Practically all, with the exception of the divisions. We shall concentrate our peace-time activities on the east and west coasts; Halifax and Esquimait. Sydney also will be kept open for some considerable time, just how long I do not know, as a store base. All the subsidiary bases which are purely war-time bases will be closed

The divisions in the various cities it is contemplated will be kept open as well as the two inland magazines.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There were quite a few subsidiary bases. The minister 'has just stated that they are to be closed. I presume that a good deal of money has been spent on each one of them. Are they just to be allowed to go, or is some arrangement being made so that the navy will still have control of them?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The physical assets at the surplus bases such as buildings, power plant and that sort of thing are turned over to War Assets Corporation for disposal. We are retaining control of the land in the event of our needing it in some future war. The same sort of thing will apply to most of the subsidiary bases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What about Shelburne?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is still being operated, but I imagine it will be closed and disposed of as well. It is true that these stations represent a substantial expenditure of money, but they were set up to fight a naval war and our main naval war was fought in the Atlantic. Like so many other war expenditures, these represent part of the cost of war. We cannot run a modern peace-time navy in the post-war if we spend all our naval appropriation in maintaining bases that we do not need in peace time. We have to make sure that our naval dollar is used to the very best advantage.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What is to be done with the docks at North Vancouver? They are barely completed. There is a depot there. Is that to be disposed of to private interests?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Those docks will be used as long as we need them for the navy and, while I cannot make any commitment, I think it is probable that they will be turned over eventually to the harbour commissioners.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
