I suppose that our contribution to whatever provision' is made under the collective security agreement for defence measures would come from our navy, army and air forces, and the stores which they might have to support their operations. Dealing with the item of armament stores, if we had some six-inch guns which were not needed for our own ships we might supply them to some other ships of a joint force under the collective agreement. I would have to be fairly general on that. The estimates which I am presenting now represent the amounts which the government is asking to defray the costs of the naval service up to March 31, 1946. I suppose from a practical point of view it is unlikely that any of the current expenditures would be devoted to the cost of some force set up under the collective agreement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The minister then anticipates that we would have two forces in that event; that we would maintain Canadian defence separately from the international pool?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I would think that we must maintain our own domestic defence force for the policing of our own territorial area, for instance, with the -appropriate staffs, establishments, and so on; and that whatever con-
Demobilization-Naval Services

tribution we might undertake to make to a world force or to a joint force would be made from that establishment. If we undertook to contribute so many men or so many ships and our domestic establishment were were not adequate to provide those in addition to what we needed for our own territorial defence we would expand our forces. That is about as definite as I can be.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Do the pay and allowances include merchant seamen in addition to the regular-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I hate to take this technical position with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, but we are proceeding item by item here. We disposed of pay and allowances some time ago. We had a long general discussion on civil salaries in which general remarks of all kinds were permissible. We have been taking the different heads item by item, and I. am reluctant to go back on the items, but I will answer my hon. friend's question. It does not include anything for merchant seamen.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Fuel for ships, $9,915,270.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Could the minister give us some particulars about this item? I presume some of the fuel would be coal, some oil, some gas, and perhaps some wood. Could the minister give us a breakdown of the figures? Could he let us know also if part of the fuel was purchased outside this country? Then I would ask the minister how the actual expenditures for last year compared with the estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
To answer the last question first, the actual expenditures for last year were $26,245,347. The estimated expenditures for last year were $27,806,604, or roughly $1,000,000 more than the amount actually spent. This item includes, in addition to fuel oil for ships' bunkers, coal for ships, diesel oil, gasoline and lubricating oil for ships. I have a break-down of items for the current fiscal year:
Fuel oil	 $ 9,565,252
Diesel oil	 358,529
Gasoline	 336.048
Steam coal	 108.879
Fuel for heating	 89,580
Lubricating oils	 448,732

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What is that fuel for heating?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
It would be coal, I suppose, and perhaps fuel oil used for heating ships as distinct from fuel used for steaming. It is all grouped into the one heading. From that total is deducted $1,000,000 which is estimated as covering a portion of future years' require-

ments, leaving a balance of $9,907,020. The cash appropriation for the first five months was $5,009,782, and the net additional requirement estimated is $4,897,238. As the committee will see from the above summary, by far the largest proportion of the amount is represented by fuel oil for the ships.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
That is the item of
$9,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is correct. The estimate represents a substantial reduction, $17,891,334, from the estimate for the previous year, which, as I indicated a moment ago, was within $1,000,000 of the actual expenditure.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Where was the fuel oil or
coal purchased?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
That is purchased by the
Department of Munitions and Supply, and I am afraid I cannot give my hon. friend the information.	.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is the old standby.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: My hon. friend the Minister of Munitions and Supply is just as capable of answering questions as I am, perhaps more so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I did not hear the minister mention anything about fuel oil or fuel for the fleet air arm. Is that not included for the aircraft and the carriers? Are they to have any fuel?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The arrangement at the
moment is that we pay the admiralty for that up to March 31. It is included in the general estimates, but there is no specific appropriation. My hon. friend will recall that we expect the first of the carriers to be commissioned about January 15 and the second perhaps six or seven months later, so that there will be a period, presumably, of some two and a half months during which provision would have to be made for the operation of that carrier.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: And the aircraft on it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Has the department disposed of any fuel as surplus anywhere?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am advised that everything not needed is reported as surplus, and we receive directions from War Assets Corporation to turn it over to commercial companies.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
But the question was, has
the department disposed of any as surplus?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I am advised that we have disposed of substantial quantities.

Demobilization-Naval Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: At what bases would there be surplus fuel?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Sydney, Halifax, Shelburne, Prince Rupert.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Under the item of fuel for
ships could the minister tell us how much per ton that fuel cost the government?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is one of the questions I am sorry to have to keep answering in the same way. The fuel is purchased by the Department of Munitions and Supply; the navy department does not purchase it. We indent, as it were, the Department of Munitions and Supply and tell them to get us so many tons of fuel. They set the price and deliver the fuel to us. If my hon. friend will make a note to ask the purchasing department what they paid for it he will be able to get the information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: At the same time they supply you with fuel, do they not also supply you with an account covering the fuel?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: They bill us from- time to time and we pay the price they set. We pay in bulk.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Therefore would it not be possible to calculate exactly what the fuel cost?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I think it would be possible, by dividing the total number of tons of fuel we have burned by the total price we have paid, to get a unit cost, but I do not know that this has been done. If I may say so, we are not particularly concerned. We do not have to drive the bargain. The Department of Munitions and Supply makes the deal and we pay the bills.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: As I understand it from the minister, the navy department pays these accounts. They do not pay the Department of Munitions and Supply; they pay the accounts direct. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: If that is so, the minister should be able to tell us who are the suppliers. I think he should answer that question and not put it over to muntions and supply.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Perhaps we could get the information, because we receive the invoices, but as I have said the purchasing department is the Department of Munitions and Supply. They keep the records; that is their job. They do the buying, and I suggest that questions as to the people from whom supplies are purchased should be directed to those who
do the purchasing. I could get the information, but I suggest it is much more efficient to get it from the. man who does the buying. If my hbn. friend insists, perhaps I could ask my staff to check up with munitions and supply, or go through the invoices; but it has been the job of the Department of Munitions and Supply to do the buying and that is the department to give the information. One of its functions is to give members of the house that information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Do you not get a credit when you turn over these supplies? Let us take the first item of $9,000,000, which we have authorized the department to spend for fuel. Supposing you turn back $1,000,000 worth of fuel, what happens? You have $9,000,000 and you require to spend only $8,000,000. Do you not get a credit?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No, we do not. It may be poor accounting, but our books will show that we have spent $9,000,000 and War Assets Cor-portion gets credit for the $1,000,000. It is the same in connection with corvettes. We show that we have spent $750,000 in round figures for a corvette, and I see by the newspapers that War Assets Corporation is selling them for $40,000 or $50,000 each.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I suggest that is not good accounting. As far as capital ships and capital expenditures go, that may be all right, but in connection with fuel and other ships' supplies I certainly think the minister's department should get credit on a one hundred per cent basis. It goes through War Assets Corporation, it goes through an independent channel; it is passed on from there to independent dealers who sell the oil to other ships. I do not think there is any accounting. The minister's department should receive credit for that and he should be able to give us that figure.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend is right, but it is not done. The net recovery in the final analysis comes back into the same pocket, the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It is not salvage to that extent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The minister said that considerable fuel had been turned back to munitions and supply Or to War Assets Corporation. Can he give us a breakdown of that in amounts? There is a different set of figures for this department from what there is for the other service departments. What is the value of gasoline, fuel oil and coal that the department has burned up, and from what places was it purchased?
Demobilization-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I have not the information here but I am advised that it can be obtained.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The public of. Canada are asking the question: what does it cost annually to run our navy? From what the minister has said it would appear they are getting the same kind of nonsense in this case that they get in connection with most questions they ask. Apparently they are not going to get a correct answer about the cost of their navy. This is just in keeping with most of the actions of this government. They must go to the Department of Munitions and Supply to get the correct answer. It is the old runaround the soldiers and everybody else are getting. The people of Canada should know what this navy is costing. When goods belonging to the navy are sold, the navy should get the credit. Otherwise we do not have a true picture.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I can understand the
Minister of National Defence for Naval Services not being able to furnish information as to where the oil has been purchased, but I think it is certainly poor accounting when the officials of his department do not know what price they paid for these different fuels.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We do know. I have given my hon. friend the gross amount. I can get him the information from naval service headquarters. We can get the number of tons of fuel oil, and that number can be divided into $9,000,000, which will give him the amount paid. It is simply a matter of arithmetic.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Tell the people of
Canada what it costs to run the navy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I understand that we are to get a break-down, of what has been turned over to War Assets Corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes; I promise that any information of that kind will be given. I hope the committee is not under any misapprehension. This is all available, some of it more readily than others. Hon. members will realize that it is almost impossible for me or for the deputy to anticipate the great variety of combinations of figures which may be asked for in committee. All I can do under such circumstances is to say that we will get the information and give it to the committee at the first available opportunity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Some questions are fairly obvious.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: But others are not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I think the minister will admit that this is quite a legitimate request.

We find that $9,000,000 is being voted, and I would think the estimates would foresee and perhaps take into consideration that there would be a credit received because some was turned over to War Assets Corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I hope I am not giving the impression that I think these questions are frivolous or foolish, because I do not mean that for a moment. I confess that I did not even know myself that some of this oil may have been turned back. I can get the information and it will be given very readily.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Would I be in order to ask that this item be allowed to stand and that we go on to another item so that the minister can get that information?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I have given an undertaking to furnish it. It has been the practice in the past, when hon. members asked for certain information which required some time to obtain, to promise that it would be made available at a future time. In this case officials will get the information as soon as pos

sible, and I will place it before the committee, either on a later item or, with the consent of the committee, when some other minister is putting through his estimates.
I think it will facilitate the progress of the business of the committee not to hold up the item. I give the formal undertaking that everything which has been asked for to-night and which can be obtained will be furnished. We are making a careful note of everything that has been asked for and it will be furnished at the first available opportunity.. I think it is certain that the discussion on this resolution will carry on for some considerable time, whether on naval estimates or otherwise, and I will see that the information is given.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Having asked the question, may I say that that is quite satisfactory to me. I would not ask that the item stand as long as the information will be provided, possibly when we are discussing one of the other service departments.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Those of us who have sat on previous committees will recall that that has been the practice in the past.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am sure the minister does not mean to suggest that we cannot revert later on to one of these items if someone has a legitimate question to ask.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The practice in the past has been to cover the items. It may be that I am unable to give the information asked for, but in each case I have undertaken to give it at a later day. I suggest with great diffidence that that is the only way we can

Demobilization-Naval Services
expect a reasonable expedition of business in the committee. If we reopen each item, then each one of two hundred odd members will have an equal right to ask other questions. If there is some matter of vital importance which has been overlooked, personally I would not want to stand on any technical ground, but once we have passed an item I would not want to see the committee revert to it for the purpose of reopening the whole matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The hon. member has referred to the practice in the past. The practice in the past has been to have a resolution dealing with each separate item. When the resolution was passed, then we were done with it. But that has not been done with these estimates. We have only the one resolution dealing with SI,365 million. It was not proposed that there be a general reopening of these items once we have discussed them, but I hope the minister is not taking a firm stand that if there is some question to be asked later about any of these items we shall not be able to ask it. I hope he is not taking the position that we cannot go back to it.
I think we are all anxious to help the minister expedite the business of this committee, but since we have this one general resolution under which we can, under our rules, raise any matter at any time, I do not think the minister should take a firm position.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Technically the leader of the opposition is perfectly right but, as he probably knows just as well as I do, in five years of dealing with these war appropriation resolutions we have invariably followed the practice which is being followed in this debate of separating the various service estimates into groups of expenditures, allowing a general discussion at the outset of each department, passing each separate group one by one and then not reverting to the particular items. That has been the practice which has been followed for five years. I agree with the hon. member that perhaps legally and technically it is perfectly open to the committee to go back to any one of these items and under those circumstances it is impossible for me to take a firm stand. I simply point out to him what has been our practice and I think it has a good deal to commend it.
I am willing to take just as much time as he wants on any one of these individual items. We are now discussing the question of [DOT] fuel, and if the committee wants to, I am prepared to discuss fuel until eleven o'clock to-night. There is no difference between setting up an item of 39,000,000 for fuel under war appropriations, as we are doing here, and having
a separate item in the civil estimates for the same amount. Under civil estimates, when we have voted an item for $9,000,000 for fuel, it would be concluded and we would not go back to it.
I agree with the leader of the opposition and I will not take any firm stand on it. Legally I think the committee is entitled to go back to any item. But I hope that, except under the most unusual circumstances, when we have passed an item I can really take it that we have finished with it and can go on to the next one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Perhaps I was the first on this side of the house to say to hon. members opposite that we would try to discipline ourselves to keep within that general practice because as the minister says if we do not do that, we should be here for a long time. But a couple of times the minister has referred to people over here going back to an item already passed. I have in mind the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. She asked about a matter that had not been dealt with, and the minister argued that the item had been passed and that he did not want a precedent established by going back to the item again. I am not suggesting that we start in and go over all the items that have been passed. There is not much difference of opinion between us on that. But I hope that the minister will not take too firm a position if some legitimate question was overlooked that should be raised.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: May I point out in closing that the leader of the opposition is the first one who has raised this question in the five years that we have been dealing with war estimates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I just want to add this, that if the minister is going to take that strong position he will be a longer time in getting through his estimates than he otherwise would be.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I am prepared to take just as much time as the committee wants to take. I will take two or three or four weeks, just as much time as the committee requires. I do not want my hon. friend to think I was attempting to be adamant. I was merely pointing out that for five years we have followed a certain practice, and1 in replying to my hon. friend the member for Qu'Appelle I was simply voicing my view as to the practice that had been established in this house. I do not think any hon. member who was here in the last session will contradict me when I say that the point which has been taken by the leader of the opposition has been taken for the first time with respect to the war appropriation.
Demobilization-Naval Services

His point is well taken; I have conceded that to him, and now having established the legal position, I express the hope that we shall continue the practice that has been followed for the past five years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: When I made my suggestion a few minutes ago that this item should stand and that the committee go on to another item I did not know that during the past five years there had -been a new procedure followed in this house because, when I sat in the house prior to the second world war, I remember that on many an occasion a minister would allow an item to stand and go on to another item, perhaps because he had not the information before him that the committee asked for or because something else necessitated1 that stand.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am prepared to do that. The only point I was making was with reference to the established practice on the war appropriation. It has been the practice, of course, sometimes to pass on to another item and give the other information asked for at a later time. I am in the hands of the committee. I do not care. It is nothing to me. I have all the time in the world.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It is not a matter of time at all. That was not the question that was raised.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I should not have said that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It is a question of whether in the event of some matter being overlooked the minister is going to permit us to go back to an item already passed. So far as I am concerned', we are willing to help to get through all these items, but we do not want to be held too strictly to the procedure the minister has just stated, because he is not in a position to argue for that in view of the way in which these war estimates have been brought before the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I should like to say a word in connection with the procedure which is now being questioned by the committee, and I wish to say it as a member of the opposition which is concerned with the close scrutiny of what is going on on the government side.
I hold in my hand a copy of the civil estimates for the current fiscal year. I remind members of the house that there are some very important items in the civil estimates and that we have not had a chance in this house to discuss civil estimates since August, 1944. While it is perfectly true that we can take all the time we want on the resolution now before the house, hon. members should realize that the more time we take on the war appropriation, the less time there will be for

the civil estimates. I have been here long enough to know the speed at which the business of the house moves and the pressure that is put on in the last two or three days of a session. Not only are there civil estimates to consider, but the order paper is full of all kinds of important legislation to come before the house, and it seems to me that those of us on the opposition side should have an interest not only in spending time on one subject but in budgeting our time so that we shall not be pushed for time when important matters come up toward the end of the session.
I would say this to the leader of the opposition, that a member who wishes to go back and ask questions that he has overlooked on some item already passed is well protected by the fact that after this resolution is passed a bill has to be introduced and given a first and second reading, go through the committee stage and come again before the house for third reading, so that there are plenty of opportunities for a member to bring up later anything he has overlooked.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that I am arguing the case of the opposition, not the case of the government, in what I am saying. Surely as members of the opposition we are interested in budgeting our time to consider the matters to come before the house, and we should agree to this procedure of passing these appropriations item by item. The leader of the opposition is perfectly right. Technically this is one resolution, but in our own interests I think we should agree to the procedure and try to expedite the business of the house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Surely the minister
did not mean-I do not think he did-that we were going to continue passing estimates in peace time in the same fashion as we did when the war was on, when we realized the uncertainties of war and gave the war departments a blank cheque. Surely the minister and the government do not expect that we are going to continue that practice, issue a blank cheque as the minister has suggested this evening. We are prepared as members of the opposition to cooperate in trying to get these items through as quickly as we can, but I think the minister was a little too stiff in his stand on the practice that has obtained in the last five war years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Perhaps we have wasted
too much time on this discussion, but I say that we were the first to offer to discipline ourselves to keep within the general procedure adopted in discussing the war appropriation. I rose only because the minister objected to some hon. member on this side asking a particular question on an item which had been passed. The item had passed before the question could very well be raised. We do not want to make a general practice of that. It is not that we want to do that at all, and I do not think there is much difference between us.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Well, let us get on with the business.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: If the hon. member for Humboldt is attempting to lecture me, may I suggest that he apply his lecture to some of his own party, because it was they who suggested that we revert to this item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I sat in the house this afternoon for two hours listening to questions coming from youth and age in the opposition, and I was surprised at the courteous way in which the Minister of National Defence answered those questions, and at the splendid way in which the information came across. I think the minister is to be commended. He is not so old as some of us but he is far wiser. I should like to pay tribute to him for his patence; and he did not have a chip on his shoulder once to-night.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I think we can join with the hon. member in the comment he has made. I am sure I can.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I think I had better rise and take a bow, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We are discussing the estimate for fuel for ships. In a statement a few minutes ago the minister said that War Assets Corporation or the Department of Munitions and Supply or some second or third party had disposed of approximately one million dollars worth of fuel oil or fuel for ships for his department.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: May I interrupt? I mentioned no amount.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The minister said, approximately a million.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I said, "a substantial amount," but I mentioned no figure, because I have no information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: At any rate the minister said that they had sold fuel for his department. A month or two afterwards he comes along and asks us to pass estimates for $9,915,270. It is amazing that, if the department's requirements for the coming year amount to over $9,000,000, they should dispose of any fuel oil in the months which have gone by. I suggest, that an explanation in that regard is due to the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Of course the answer to that one is fairly obvious. We shall have surpluses at certain places at certain times, and I do not know that it would be either in the [DOT] interests of the navy or of would-be consumers of fuel-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What does the minister mean by that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We may have at Halifax to-day a surplus of fuel oil. Let us say for the sake of argument that we are not going to need that fuel for two or three months. We therefore advise munitions and supply that we have this surplus and they dispose of it. Four months later we need some more and we make another purchase. But we overestimated our requirements. We obviously made commitments and purchased, before the termination of the Japanese war, beyond our immediate needs. That is the answer as far as that is concerned. We have a surplus in certain ports, and we have to purchase in others. But we would not go on buying fuel which we did not use.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Yes, but the department must have a great storage capacity, has it not?
Demobilization-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We have a substantial storage capacity. But the point I made a moment ago is that it is not in the interests of the community where there is a shortage of fuel supplies to keep for three or four months supplies which we are not going to need; it is better to allow them to be used in the district in which they may be located, replacing them from later shipments. I cannot speak from any personal knowledge of what was done, but that is the general explanation given me by the deputy minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What loss would you take per ton on sales you have made? I assume that there is a loss.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I could not say whether there would be any loss. I doubt whether there would be. They dispose of the fuel at the current market price. As my hon. friend knows, all these items are in short supply. The problem is not to have a surplus of coal but to have enough, and pretty much the same principle applies to gasoline and fuel oil.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What about handling charges?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There may be some loss in handling charges, that is * true.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Ships of other nations call at Canadian ports and refuel. What arrangements have been made by the department with other nations with respect to this matter? Is there anything in these items which would cover transactions of that sort?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I do not know that these estimates contain any specific items for that. I am advised that during the war, at points like Newfoundland, where probably the only available supplies would be naval supplies, we would supply ships of the Royal Navy, for instance, and charge them with the cost of the fuel supplied, but according to my information that was not done on a substantial scale.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Since I was the unfortunate individual who raised this question, I want first to say that I am satisfied with the minister's explanation. He told us precisely where we could get the information desired. When ** asked the question I was merely looking fin information. Had I ever thought that the discussion of that one little point would last this long I would never have brought it forward. However, I want to thank the minister for his explanation as to where we can get that information, and I hope the incident will be considered closed.
[Mr Cockeram.J

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I have just one or two observations to make. First, I should like to join with the hon. member for Fort William, in this sense, that I appreciate the courtesy of the minister, but I cannot understand why the hon. member said he was surprised at it. After all, I do not think he should be surprised; I think the minister simply treats us as we like to be treated.
We have been speaking of fuel for ships, and I understand that requirements are less because there are fewer corvettes and so forth. But when you sell the fuel back to the Department of Munitions and Supply, the credit balance should be the same. There might be a shrinkage, but I cannot imagine any depreciation in the value. If you made a reasonably good purchase you should get the same amount of money back. So that probably that point was not well presented.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I, too, might perhaps associate myself to a certain extent in the compliment paid by the hon. member for Fort William, but I should like to point out that the minister has SI,300 million involved, and I could wear a smile for quite a long time for SI,300 million.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Only $299 million, just a bagatelle.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Some bagatelle. However, the point I raise in connection with that is that the minister has yet to give us information, in order to complete the picture, as to the amount which might be accounted a re-credit for the disposal of certain items by War Assets Corporation; that is, in connection with the sale of fuel. In order that we may have the picture clearly, would he be prepared-possibly he may be able to do it for the rest of the items of the navy and for the same items under the army-to get the same information and let us have it, in connection with other items? The next item we come to is, "acquisition, construction, charter, repairs and upkeep of ships," and I can foresee that there might be quite a heavy run of disposal of these stores through War Assets Corporation. I believe we would be very much interested in knowing whether there is a large sum which we can re-credit to the department, in connection with the passing of these estimates; whether, for instance, there will be a substantial amount off that $50,000,000, and off the next items. To save us asking each time an item comes up, perhaps the minister can give us an undertaking on. that matter now'.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The position I am in is this.
I can tell the committee what particular-

Demobilization-Naval Services
physical items were declared surplus, but I cannot tell the committee what those items realized after being sold by War Assets Corporation, because, as I explained earlier, the system of accounting, rightly or wrongly, does not credit the navy appropriation account with the amounts. I could tell the committee what items were declared surplus or have already been declared surplus under these particular items. I think I should point out that under certain headings it might involve a considerable amount of work to get the information accurately. Under fuel it would be comparatively easy because that is dealt with in bulk, but as regards miscellaneous stores and equipment I do not know how easy it would be. The deputy minister tells me that there are literally thousands of declarations on surplus items. Perhaps the same information in total might be obtained under munitions and supply estimates or some appropriate item by asking what amounts had been realized by War Assets Corporation from the disposal of surplus naval stores. Probably that information in total would be available readily.

speechtext:
I am not prepared to table the findings of the courts of inquiry themselves, on the basis that those documents are never tabled in parliament, but I shall be glad to give the committee a statement as to the circumstances surrounding the sinking of the three yachts, and a summary of the findings of the court of inquiry. If the committee would wait a moment, perhaps I have the memorandum here.
The first one to which the hon. member referred was the Otter. His Majesty's Canadian ship Otter caught fire and foundered with heavy loss of life off Halifax. The charge is that there was danger of fire because of faulty wiring in this ship. I may say this was the allegation that was made in connection with the charges to which my hon. friend refers- danger of fire because it is said that faulty wiring in this ship had been pointed out to the proper authorities verbally and in writing and by signal on various occasions during the period of her service. It is charged that only a few days before the disaster the commanding officer of H.M.C.S. Otter was warned by an officer of long experience that 47696-99
[DOT] it was his duty to refuse to proceed to sea until his ship had been rewired. Here are the facts. The Otter sank on March 26, 1941 as a result of a fire. A naval board of inquiry was immediately convened to make a full inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the loss of the vessel. While the cause of the fire could not be definitely ascertained, the board expressed the opinion, after examining all relevant witnesses, that the fire was caused by the sudden overloading of one of the vessel's generators.
Earlier in her commission the ship had been found to have faulty wiring and she was rewired in the summer of 1940 by Messrs. Lambert, German and Milne, naval architects of Montreal. In January, 1941, her wiring was again checked in Halifax. The board of inquiry adduced no evidence to indicate that the wiring of the ship was at fault. The commanding officer of the vessel, Lieutenant D. S. Mossman, R.C.NR., who was questioned at considerable length made no reference to the alleged warning.
The second case was the Raccoon. The charges were that the Raccoon was known to be considered unseaworthy by experienced officers long before the day she disappeared into the gulf of St. Lawrence. There were other incidents. It is said that local fishermen at certain seaports reported) that she was detached for patrol and rescue duties there, but was considered so unseaworthy that during bad weather she was anchored under the lee of an island, while they, the Nova Scotia fishermen, had to go to sea to rescue merchant seamen whose ships had been torpedoed off our coast. There is no information, however, regarding any incident in which the Raccoon was forced to anchor as suggested.
It can be stated that the yachts acquired by the Royal Canadian Navy as stop-gap patrol vessels, that is to say, pending the completion of new construction escort vessels, were the most seaworthy of suitable vessels available at that time. They were inspected before commissioning and refitted from time to time. The disappearance of the Raccoon was not a matter of seaworthiness; the vessel was torpedoed by an enemy submarine.
It is alleged that in the case of the Bras d'Or, her commander, an experienced officer, was said to have protested that he was far from satisfied) with the condition of the ship's boilers, even after the refit that was completed shortly before she foundered. It is alleged that that was why an engineer overseer officer was sent specially from Quebec to inquire into the protests of the officer commanding.	,

Demobilization-Naval Services

The facts in connection with the matter are as follows. His Majesty's Canadian Ship Bras d'Or was lost on October 19, 1940. She had been completely refitted shortly before that day, but because her boilers had previously given trouble an engineer overseer officer was sent to observe them in operation. A naval board of inquiry was convened, to make a full inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the loss of the vessel. After examining all relevant witnesses, the board expressed the opinion that the ship was apparently in good condition when refitted but that she had been grounded off Rimouski just over twenty-four hours before she sank. This grounding was not reported by her commanding officer, Lieutenant Charles A. Hornsby, R.C.N.R., presumably because of his zeal to carry out shadowing orders which had just been received. While no apparent damage was caused by the grounding, the board was of opinion that the strain suffered at that time was the chief contributory factor in her loss during rough weather on October 19.

Perhaps I had better give

We are asking for provision this year of $29,645,280 as compared with an estimate last year of $42,678,967 and an actual expenditure of $49,091,842. This item is made up of naval stores; small boats; antisubmarine equipment; fire fighting equipment; charts; miscellaneous special equipment; training equipment; photographic equipment; furniture and galley equipment; motor vehicles; harbour defences. Of the total requested, $18,152,000 represents carryover of unliquidated liabilities from 1944-45, and $7,568,338 represents estimated expenditures to August 31, 1945. Provision has also been made for the liquidation during the seven months' period ending March 31, 1946, of commitments entered into during the first five months of this fiscal year, and for stores of the Canadian naval air service, most of which are not in stock. The amount provided for harbour defences is wholly for the liquidation of unpaid accounts and expenditures already made.
It will be noted that the amount requested this year is approximately $13,000,000 less than was requested in the estimates of 1944-45 and approximately $19,500,000 less than the amount actually spent during that year. That reduction is reflected in the drop from the peak buying which was under way to equip new ships in 1944-45 and to procure more modem technical equipment for anti-submarine detection, harbour defences and life-saving gear; also to replace other equipment which was wearing out or was found to be not up to the standard required, particularly in the anticipated operations in the Pacific where new tactics had developed.
