speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: These craft, as well as any other items of this kind, are offered to the other defence departments before being declared surplus. That was the case with these Fairmiles, but boats that use 100 gallons of high octant gas an hour are not very good boats for braining or patrol purposes in peace time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Were they considered to be efficient patrol boats by the naval engineers?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am advised that they were considered to be efficient patrol boats for the purpose for which they were designed in war time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What was that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Close escort work. The trip I had on one was out of Gaspe harbour, and they were operating between Gaspe and Anticosti and between Gaspe and Newfoundland. They were escorting convoys in those waters.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is there any record that they encountered U-boats or enemy vessels? I understand that they have a speed of only twenty-four knots.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Only twenty-four knots? That is quite1 a speed.

Demobilization-Naval Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is not to be compared with the speed' of the boats that were used around the English shores.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I do not know what speed they make; I doubt if they make as much as twenty-four knots.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: How many different types of engines were tried out in these boats?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Two types, the Sterling and the Hall Scott.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Just two types?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Were both found satisfactory, or was there trouble about breaking jackets when the boats were speeded up?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Both were satisfactory, but one which was obtained in the United States became unprocurable.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Were no Rolls-Royce engines installed in Fairmiies in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: On the question of the speed of Fairmiies I might mention that those equipped with the Hall Scott engine could do something like eighteen knots and those equipped with the Sterling, twenty-two knots. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard asked if any other department had taken any of those ships. I can inform him that the R.C.M.P. have taken' nine, if not eleven Fairmiies..

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I think the situation is not quite as good as the hon. member for New . Westminster would have us believe. According to press reports, seven of these Fairmiies were sold to Thomas F. Hamilton of Malibu club, Princess Louise inlet. One was reported sold for a private yacht to Mr. Garfield Weston, and one to some other person. In cases like that, there is no excuse for selling these boats for $3,000, and there should be some control over War Assets Corporation to prevent sales of that kind from being made.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I suggest that that question should be directed to the minister in charge of War Assets Corporation. Let me tell my hon. friend that no one will use any one of these Fairmiies as a private yacht without putting in another engine because, as they are now, you cannot hear yourself think on board. I have been in them, and the hon. member for Gaspe will bear me out when I say that no one will use a Fairmile as a private yacht without putting in a new engine.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Now that the war is over, is it necessary to keep these degaussing stations going?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I do not know if I can answer that question. The degaussing station is being moved away from Vancouver, and the question whether it will be maintained anywhere else is under consideration. I will make inquiry from the chief of the naval staff and find out what the staff view is.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Do navy blankets come under this item for miscellaneous stores?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That comes under item 5, for personnel supplies. But if my hon. friend wants information about it I will consider his question as coming under this item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I just wanted to ask if these surplus blankets were sold for twenty-five cents apiece?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I have to repeat the answer I have often given that the navy does not sell anything. We declare them surplus and they are turned over to the crown assets allocation committeee, which turns them over to War Assets Corporation, which sells them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: This country is being asked to contribute clothing for the peoples of the overrun countries of Europe, and if these blankets were sold at twenty-five cents apiece they certainly should not have been sold for that price.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know that they were sold for twenty-five cents a piece?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No. I asked the question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Before making such a statement, my hon. friend should make sure of his

facts.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I was informed that they were sold for twenty-five cents apiece, and if they were I say that it is ridiculous under those circumstances to ask this country to supply clothing for the peoples of Europe when this material could have been made available to them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
In the decommissioning of ships, I presume that some dismantling takes place before decommissioning. Can the minister give us any idea how much equipment is removed from a ship before it is turned over to War Assets Corporation? I presume they would remove the guns, the radar and the wireless. Do they remove the power plant, the auxiliary electrical machinery and equipment such as that?
Demobilization-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: As my hon. friend has indicated, secret equipment is removed and must be destroyed or mutilated to preserve secrecy. Sto'res and equipment for which the navy has a continuing need are removed. In all other cases the stores and equipment are left on board and War Assets Corporation is supplied with an inventory of these stores. That practice serves two purposes. First, it obviates the necessity of the naval service removing and storing equipment for which they have no need, and, second, it materially assists War Assets Corporation in making a sale because the ship then contains a great deal of equipment necessary for running purposes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: A considerable amount of money was spent in the war to provide merchant ships with guns and other protection from the enemy. What has been done with that material?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It was taken off the ships and put back into naval stores or naval ordnance.	.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous stores and services, $10,844,578.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The provision made this year is $10,844,578 as against $8,873,210 in the preceding year and actual expenditures in the preceding year of $8,268,811. While this item includes such sundry expenses as printing and stationery, books for service use, reference books, typewriters and office machines, laundry and dry cleaning, storekeeping materials, inspection and testing of water for ships, by far the largest and most significant item is wages, which account for $8,472,623. Wages are paid to civilian storekeepers, magazine workers, laundry assistants, motor vehicle operators and mechanics and other monthly paid and hourly paid civilian employees other than civil servants, dockyard tradesmen, labourers and maintenance personnel. As in the case of civil servants, dockyard workers and maintenance personnel, provision has to be made for replacement of naval personnel in cases where the functions and activities in which naval personnel were engaged must continue. This item is one which would include amounts for services such as those referred to by the hon. member for Camrose earlier in the discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Where this $8,000,000 is paid to other than regular members of the naval forces, to permanent civil servants, is the money paid by the civil service department to which they originally belonged, or is it paid by the naval department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Expenditures for civil service-I use that term in the .broad sense- come under item 1, civil salaries. The estimated amount is about $7,000,000. The amount here is for civil employees who are outside that category and, as I indicated in my explanatory statement, are storekeepers, magazine workers, laundry assistants, that type of employee, a good many of whom would be on hourly rates of pay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Would they be, in the main, technical men?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No, I would not think they would be technical men; they would be, go to speak, miscellaneous employees, say workers in bakeries-I mention that because I went through some of the naval bakeries- also storekeepers, people working at, for instance, Bedford magazine, other workers in the Renous and Kamloops magazines, all kinds of odds and ends of civilian workers. I do not use the term "odds and ends" in any derogatory sense, but miscellaneous types of workers, largely on hourly rates of pay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is that the reason why this is distinguished from item 1, because in item 1 you have not only civil salaries but wages. I should like to be certain that there is no chance of a duplication. You speak of wages for workers of miscellaneous types, but you have "wages" up above. What would the first item of wages include?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: To get the correct picture as to the amount paid in salaries and wages of civilian personnel, if I may so describe them, one should take the $7,000,000 in item 1, plus the $8,000,000 which is included in this item, making a total in round figures of $15,000,000, plus the amounts included under construction and repairs of ships and under maintenance of above establishments. That gives the over-all picture with respect to salary and wage payments to civilian employees, some of whom are straight civil servants employed through the civil service commission, some of whom are temporaries whose engagement is subject to approval by the civil service commission, some of whom are labourers engaged to work in magazines, dockyards and shipyards.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
It is very difficult for us to make any check on expenditures of this kind. Can the minister give us any particulars of what relationship this cost totalling $15,000,000, of which he has just spoken, bears to the cost of other years, and particularly with reference to how much it has been reduced in the current year?

Demobilization-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The amounts seem very large. I do not emphasize the point with any critical intent, but an increase of $2,000,000 over last year in a total expenditure of $15,000,000, at a time when such duties as the minister has explained should be abating rather than increasing, seems rather high. The fact that the total cost of the first six months is approximately $3,500,000, and yet the appropriation is about $15,000,000, is hard to understand.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No; I am only giving the three millions against the ten millions here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I suppose the ratio with the civil service is similar under the other item.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No; under the other item the ratio is higher, about forty-six per cent as against thirty-two per cent here. My hon. friend's question is a perfectly appropriate one. It is an increase which it is quite proper should be queried. But I would point out to the committee that this year involves the liquidation and de-storing of the major portion of our navy, including all those small ships we are laying up, and that involves a great deal of work by temporary civilian employees. We shall do as much of it as we can, of course, with service personnel who are or have to be kept in the navy. But in preparing the estimates it was contemplated that to do this work we must make a provision for substantial expenditures, which would, of course, not be recurring expenditures.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It does seem to me strange, however; that they should be increasing at this time, because one would think that he would need more civilian employees of this kind in building, equipping, maintaining and serving the naval force through the period we have gone through, rather than that the number would then be cut down. I think the point does reflect to some degree at least upon what appears to be tardiness in relieving the personnel of the civilian employees under this section. I do not like to go into any more detail, but the minister has not given us very much on which we can base any judgment as to the sufficiency or efficiency of the cutting down of expenditure in this regard. I think the minister would be well advised if he had more particulars on this item to give us.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It is pretty hard to give more particulars. Perhaps I could get some more.- I have given the amount actually expended in six months, which is only $3,500,000. If that rate is not exceeded the total expenditure will be seven instead of the ten million which is shown here. We may have been unduly careful in estimating increased civilian expenditures. I can only assure the committee that I am convinced that the navy is using every effort to get the work done as cheaply as possible, but it must be done either by service personnel or by civilian personnel. If it is done by service personnel it will be reflected in pay and allowances; if it is done by civilian personnel it will be reflected in this item together with the item of civil salaries and also items under repairs, et cetera, of ships.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I notice that this item includes the heading "teletype rental". Would the minister explain the nature and extent of the proposed service for this year, the cost, and the companies or persons to whom this money for teletype rental is proposed to go?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I shall see if I have that information here. I am afraid I shall have to ask my hon. friend to allow that question to stand. This information is available, it is in the books of the department, but it is not broken down in the figures I have before me. That is one of the many services the navy obtains, and I shall get the information as to what is included in those estimates for teletype services during the current fiscal year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I have a question I should like to ask the minister which relates perhaps to all the items rather than just to this one. Of these naval expenditures, is not a certain large proportion of them paid to the Department of Munitions and Supply, and is it
Demobilization-Naval Services

really not a government book entry, rather than being paid direct by the department for naval services to the contractors?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No; we pay the supplier direct. We indent the Department of Munitions and Supply to do the purchasing. They make the contract and we receive the invoice and pay the supplier direct, I am advised.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The next item is:	-
Sundries-postage, pilotage, prize funds and rehabilitation grant, $10,033,446.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The provision asked for in the current year is 810,033,446 as against a provision asked for last year of $2,748,101, an increase of $7,285,345 in the estimates. The actual expenditures last year under this item were $2,188,764. Provision is made under this head for numerous small expenditures such as telephone, telegrams, cables, postage, pilotage, funeral expenses, bonding, premiums, tuition fees for naval officers undergoing courses in the United Kingdom, and other items not otherwise provided) for. The one large item included in the total is provision for rehabilitation grants, which amounts to $8,751,132, out of a total of $10,033,446. This item represents one month's pay for each officer and1 rating discharged from the service and is in addition to the plain clothes gratuity of $100 paid to each dischargee and included in the provision for pay and' allowances and in addition to the war service gratuities and credits paid by the Department of Veterans Affairs. The remainder under sundry expenses will, of course, show a considerable reduction on account of the over-all reduction in naval operations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Can the minister give the particulars of the various items in this $10 million in relation to actual expenditures last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The actual expenditures last year under this heading amounted to $2,188,764. We are asking for $10,033,446 this year, and if we deduct provision for rehabilitation grants the net balance amounts to $1,282,314 as against the $2,188,764 actually expended last year, a reduction of something under $1 million.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What do the words "prize funds" in this connection mean?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I have not that here. It is a small item amounting to $500 to provide prize money for proficiency in gunnery, pistol shooting and so on under the authority of certain regulations.
(Mr. Merritt.]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It has nothing to do with prize ships?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Who pays that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: How is the prize money for captured ships accounted for?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I understand that certain salvage and prize money is received for rescuing ships, but what disposition is mgde of it I do not know. Perhaps some other member of the committee is better informed than I am. I believe it has a long traditional background in the Royal Navy, but what the basis is I freely confess I do not know. Perhaps the hon. member for Yale can tell us.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I do not pretend to know much about it, but I always understood that the exchequer court arranges the sale and that the funds derived from the sale are divided into certain proportions. As the minister says, it goes back into antiquity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
It is perhaps an unfair
discrimination that this money should be paid for proficiency in gunnery. In the army the unfortunate officers were always expected to put up the money to pay the prizes for shooting, and I do not see why the navy should have a special fund provided by the government. However, we can let it go, seeing it is only $500.
There are two other items which I wish the minister would explain. I do not understand why the navy should have pilotage, particularly in war time. Another question is this: On October 22, in reply to a question by the hon. member for York South with respect to the increase from two to ten million, the minister stated that it included thirty days pay. At page 1385 of Hansard he stated that every department puts it in-that is, this thirty days' rehabilitation grant-although all ' might not put it under the same heading. I have studied the items for the other departments; I have looked at the break-down for air services and can find no record there of any such item. There is a decrease in nearly every item under the air force except item 9.
I do not think the rehabilitation and thirty days pay could come under that. Can the minister explain this difference in accounting?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I have not studied the air force estimates. It might have been well to include under item 2, pay and allowances, where there is a big reduction from the previous year, in which case this reduction would have been less. We have included it in the navy under the heading of "sundries". I do

Demobilization-Naval Services
not know why. It is the same item as is included in the estimates of all the other services. When my own army estimates are up I will indicate the item under which it is placed, and under the air estimates my colleague will be glad to advise the committee what particular item the rehabilitation grant comes under and what it amounts to in the case of the air force. It will be greater than $8 million.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I would appreciate some measure of uniformity. As regards pilotage, why should the navy pay pilotage to anyone, particularly in war time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I cannot tell why they have to but they do. Expenditure for pilotage in 1944-45 was $86,797.46 for 125 ships, or an average of 8695 per ship. I see that there is included in the estimates an amount of $6,000 to cover ten ships which it is estimated1 will pass through the Panama canal at an average cost of $500 per ship. I suppose they have thrown in an additional $1,000 for good measure.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: If my hon. friend wants more information about pilotage, I may say it is paid to naval officers when their ships are in inland waters where a civilian pilot is required. Instead of putting on a civilian pilot at so much a mile, the navigating officer and the captain of the ship are entitled to take charge of the safety of the ship and claim pilotage, which is much less than the pilotage paid to civilian pilots, and therefore the navy department is saving quite a lot of money there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Does the officer turn the
money over to the prize fund?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No; he keeps it for himself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Before the item carries I
should like to bring to the attention of the ministry once again our request that a standing committee of the house be set up on defence matters. When the war appropriation measure first came up for consideration we made that request and I think the idea was approved by all parties in the house. When the minister dealt with it he left the impression with me at least that he would wait until next session to set up this committee. I am not asking that the committee function during the present session, for the defence estimates will be passed in a few days. I think it will be in the interest of both the members of the house and the people of the country that such a committee should be set up. I suggest that the decision be made fairly soon and provision made for a change of the rules so that 47696-100
the committee could be set up and the members actually named. If that were done, the members who were on the committee could be paying particular attention to defence matters from now until the next session. They would acquire a great deal of information which otherwise they might not get; further, the officers of the forces would know for a matter of some months that they would have to appear before this committee, and furthermore, and even more important, they would know that they would have the support of the committee and of the Canadian people.
Under present conditions I think it is of vital importance that the house and the Canadian people should stand behind the defence forces to a far greater degree than has been the case in the past. I believe that end will be accomplished in the most direct way if provision is made for this committee within the next two or three weeks instead of waiting until the opening of a new session, when there would be delay, and the question might have to be argued all over again; the result would be that the committee could not do effective work for perhaps some weeks or even months after the new session opened. Therefore we suggest that the government make provision for naming the committee in the very near future.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Again I thank my hon.
friend for that suggestion. As he knows, I am very sympathetic to it. Personally, I shall see that it is given active consideration at a very early day.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I wish to make an observation in connection with the statement made by the hon. member for Gaspe regarding fees paid to pilots. He said that it was very much less than those paid to civilian pilots. I wish to point out to him and to the minister that civilian pilots operate under the Department of Transport. They depend entirely upon their fees, while the charges made by the naval officers who take over the ships in inland waters are in addition to their regular salaries. I think the hon. member made an unfair comparison.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I agree with what my
hon. friend says, but he must remember that the ships were not operating only in Canada. I myself have done some pilotage in Bermuda and in Northern Ireland, getting into Londonderry. It is only fair to the naval officer who is in charge of the ship, as commanding officer or navigation officer, because under the regulations the navigating officer is responsible for the safe navigation of the ship. He is responsible for the safety of his ship . even if he has a civilian pilot on board. He

Demobilization-Naval Services

is still in charge of the ship, and if anything happens to it he is held responsible for it. Therefore he is the man who deserves to get the money. I can tell my hon. friend I went up to Quebec and took over a ship from the Morton Engineering company. I did not take on a pilot from Quebec to Father Point. I got $35 for it, including the trials between Quebec and the Saguenay river for about ten days, besides the trip from Quebec to Father Point. I got $35 for all this work, which means that besides standing my watch of four hours I had to be on the bridge all the time. If we had taken a civilian pilot on board it would have cost the naval department, or they would have received a bill for something like $250 or $300. I think the naval * officer, besides having charge of his own ship, even if there is a civilian pilot on board, is entitled to get that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am not disputing the fact that the safety of the ship is in the hands of the officer, but I was pointing out that the hon. member was unfair to the civilian pilot who depends entirely on his fees. He comes under the Department of Transport.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I should like to table a copy of the order in council regarding military transportation rates which I promised the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) this afternoon.
PRIVILEGE-Mr. McILRAITH

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege affecting myself and arising out of an item that appears in the Ottawa Journal of to-day. The item is as follows:
Mr. George Mcllraith suggests the parliamentary committee on foreign affairs should hold its meetings in private. This secrecy stuff, permitted during the war, must be stamped out in peace. A parliamentary committee is set up simply to facilitate discussion of a complicated subject. It should meet in public, as does the Commons for which it is acting.
i might point out that there is no parliamentary committee on foreign affairs. I presume it was intended to refer to the standing committee of the House of Commons on external affairs. In any event I at no time suggested that the committee should hold its meetings in private. The item is therefore wholly without foundation.
On motion of Mr. Usley the house adjourned at 1053 p.m.

Monday, October 29, 1945.
